name: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate

lead: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate is a water-soluble oil in which glycerol carries three beta-hydroxybutyrate groups, one of the ketone bodies. It is discussed as an exogenous ketone source, in the fat-loss and metabolism category.
The human studies registered for it are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers; no efficacy trials for fat loss or appearance appear in the sources.

paras: After ingestion the ester groups are expected to be cleaved by lipases and esterases, releasing beta-hydroxybutyrate and glycerol into the circulation, where tissues can burn the ketone.

A 2025 toxicology package sponsored for novel-food use reported no genotoxicity and no adverse effects in a 90-day rat study. Human safety data are limited, and the compound is the subject of a pending EU novel-food application, not an authorization.

studies.title: Ketone body therapy: from the ketogenic diet to the oral administration of ketone ester.

lead: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate (3GHB, also tri-betahydroxybutyrin) is a synthetic triglyceride in which glycerol is fully esterified with beta-hydroxybutyric acid, a ketone body. It has the formula C15H26O9 and is a water-soluble clear oil.[1] It is not itself a ketone.[1]

Its synthesis and a seven-day infusion in rats were reported in 1997 by Birkhahn and colleagues, with support from Eastman Chemical Company, as a candidate parenteral nutrient.[1] It is discussed alongside ketone esters and salts as an exogenous ketone, a category reviewed in the context of ketone body therapy.[1][2][3]
Human studies registered for the compound are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers, not efficacy trials.[1] The sources reviewed contain no study of it for fat loss or appearance.
infobox: EU novel-food application pending; not authorized

paras: After oral exposure, the beta-hydroxybutyrate groups are expected to be cleaved from the glycerol backbone by gut lipases and esterases and released into the circulation.[1] Ketone bodies can then be oxidized by peripheral tissues.[2]

In 1997 Ronald Birkhahn, Charles McCombs, Robert Clemens and John Hubbs reported synthesizing the glycerides and a seven-day intravenous infusion in rats; a US patent the same year describes producing the water-soluble esters for use as a parenteral nutrient.[1]

A completed 2017 pharmacokinetic study in 18 men aged 60 or older compared single oral doses of three sizes, and a later crossover study compares the triester with a ketone monoester and a ketone salt in healthy adults; neither has posted results.[1] No efficacy trial for any condition is registered, and none addresses appearance or body composition.[1]

A 2025 guideline toxicology package, sponsored for novel-food use, found the compound non-genotoxic and reported no adverse effects in a 90-day rat dietary study, with a stated no-observed-adverse-effect level of 1,193 mg/kg body weight per day.[1] NeuroEnergy Ventures has applied to authorize it in the European Union as a novel-food ingredient for foods for special medical purposes; the Commission summary describes an ongoing application, not an authorization.[1]

timeline.event: Synthesis and rat infusion study reported by Birkhahn and colleagues; US patent issued.[1]
